title: Probabilistic debounce layer and shadow autoscaler for cold-start resilience
creator: Evelyn Zhang
description:
Summary: After a capacity degradation incident on 2025-01-04 where an HPA/KEDA stack interpreted bursty probe noise as sustained load, many inference hosts scaled up aggressively and then rapidly scaled down, causing cold-start latency spikes and a visible increase in 95th/99th percentile tail latency for the Redwood hosted API. This ticket tracks the investigation findings and implements a probabilistic debounce layer plus a shadow autoscaler to avoid false positives, reduce oscillation, and improve cold-start resilience.

Incident timeline (high level):
- 2025-01-04 02:13 UTC: Customer-facing latency alerts (console.slo/latency-95) triggered.
- 02:15 UTC: Autoscaler reacted to KEDA trigger bursts and HPA churn; provisioning started.
- 02:22 UTC: Warm pools were preempted by rapid scale-down; cold starts increased error budget consumption.
- 03:10 UTC: Mitigations: increased HPA stabilization window and manually bumped warm-pool min size.
- 2025-01-05: Post-incident work began; root-cause analysis started.

Root cause: A recent change in the scaler's trigger aggregation decreased smoothing (probabilistic window width reduced) to optimize for latency at low load. Under high-variance arrival patterns this produced transient high trigger scores which KEDA treated as legitimate spikes. The HPA's default stabilization window was insufficient to absorb short bursts, and warm-pool eviction policies were too aggressive when scale-down signals persisted for multiple minutes.

Key findings:
- Probe noise and short burst arrivals account for ~62% of scale-up events during the incident window (dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/board/autoscale-incident-0104).
- The scaler model lacked a burst classifier — it used a simple exponential smoothing that under-reacted to persistent spikes but over-reacted to high kurtosis bursts.
- Rapid scale-down policy did not account for pending KV cache population time, so many replicas were removed before they served critical prefix-heavy requests (cold-start penalty).

Design decisions:
1) Implement a probabilistic debounce layer before emitting a KEDA trigger: the layer computes a burst-score and schedules a probabilistic suppression on scale signals that are below an adaptive threshold. The probability is a sigmoid of burst intensity and recent success rate.
2) Add a shadow autoscaler that runs in parallel to the primary HPA: it observes longer windows and flags suspiciously noisy signals to the control plane without immediately changing replicas. When the shadow and primary disagree, the control plane will bias toward the shadow when cold-start risk is high.
3) Tune warm-pool eviction to respect a minimum-preserve window and add a grace period for replicas with populated KV caches.
4) Provide an operator flag (runtime config) to enable conservative mode per-customer for those with strict latency SLOs.

Action items (implementation plan):
- A1: Prototype probabilistic debounce algorithm in the autoscaler module (ENG) — implement feature branch and unit tests. Acceptance: deterministic unit tests for probability curve and burst scoring. (Owner: Ravi)
- A2: Build a shadow autoscaler component that exposes disagreement metrics and an API for the control plane to query consensus. Acceptance: shadow emits metrics and a sample-consensus endpoint. (Owner: Evelyn)
- A3: Change warm-pool lifecycle to add a 3-minute preserve window and KV-populated marker that prevents eviction for warmed nodes. Acceptance: integration test demonstrating no eviction within preserve window. (Owner: Core infra)
- A4: Add new dashboards and alerting (slo/scale-disagreement, slo/warm-pool-evictions) and a synthetic benchmark to validate cold-start regression before rollout. (Owner: Observability)
- A5: Run a canary rollout to 10% of capacity with conservative mode enabled for a small set of customers (QA + prod shadow). Monitor for missed scale-ups and tail latency. (Owner: SRE/Product)

Acceptance criteria:
- 30-day rolling reduction of median scale churn events by >=40%.
- No increase in 99th percentile token latency beyond 5% for canary customers.
- Warm-pool evictions reduced to <2 per week for canary group.

Rollout & rollback plan:
- Stage 1: Deploy debounce layer in opt-in mode and run shadow autoscaler for 48 hours (no control plane effect).
- Stage 2: Enable consensus-bias for canary group (10% traffic) and monitor for 72 hours.
- Stage 3: Gradually expand to 50%, then 100% if metrics stable.
- Rollback: Flip runtime flag to disable debounce and shadow, revert warm-pool policy via feature toggle. Automated rollback if 99th percentile latency regresses >10% within 1 hour.

Monitoring & follow-ups:
- New metrics: autoscaler.debounce.probability, autoscaler.shadow.disagreement, warmpool.eviction.delay.
- Dashboards and playbook updated: Confluence doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/IRON/Autoscale+Debounce+Playbook
- Post-rollout review scheduled: 2025-03-10.

Notes on trade-offs:
- Probabilistic suppression can delay legitimate scale-ups for very short bursts; shadow autoscaler mitigates by providing longer-window consensus.
- Adding more conservative warm-pool retention increases cost but preserves latency SLOs; default is conservative mode off, enterprise customers can opt in.
